title: Asking Price
passage:
A seaside season does not end on a date. It thins, and then one week the chairs stay in. In a good July week three hundred and forty of them go out on the east beach at a pound and ten pence a day, and the pitch does a ___(1)___ trade from eleven until the light goes. On the last Tuesday of September the racks under the arches held three hundred and thirty-six chairs that had ___(2)___ there since breakfast, and the tin took four pounds forty.

What the pitch charges for and what it does are not the same thing. In one hour of that Tuesday its attendant was asked where the lavatory was, whether the tide was coming in, when the last bus left for the station, and whether anybody had handed in a red shoe. She was also asked to watch a bag, a thing you ask of somebody who will still be there.

The hire is the whole of the transaction, and it has risen by ten pence in a decade. ___(3)___, the pitch is the one staffed thing on the mile between the pier and the sailing club, and Carol Gregson the one person on it who is stationary and paid. She has worked it for nine seasons. The chairs are in two stripe patterns, after a 2019 replacement batch came in the wrong blue, and that is how the stacks are told apart. Pressed on whether she minds the questions, she ___(4)___ that in August they are an interruption and by late September most of the job, a description rather than a complaint.

The town has tried providing the same thing directly. A seafront information point opened on the promenade in 2018, with a counter, a leaflet rack and a paid assistant. It was well signed and it was free, but it was ___(5)___ used, and it shut after its second summer. The leaflets were not the problem. A counter has to be approached, and approaching one is a decision you have to justify; a chair you have paid for has done the approaching for you. Gregson would not put it that way. Asked why people ask her things, she said it is because she stands still and they do not. The racks come in during the second week of October, and the firm that stacks them does the beach huts.
– Desmond Gaddermoor

questions.rationale: Key D. The frame is the fixed English collocation to do a brisk trade, which is what a busy stall or hire pitch does over a stretch of hours; the surrounding clause, from eleven until the light goes, supplies exactly the sustained-busy reading that collocation carries, and brisk is the only one of the four words that combines with trade in that sense. A (hasty) is a collocation misfit: right part of speech, same semantic field, but a hasty trade would describe one transaction done in a hurry, and there is no single transaction in the frame. B (rapid) is the same misfit in a neutral register; rapid trade belongs to markets moving quickly, not to a pitch taking money steadily all afternoon, and it fights the leisurely time adverbial. C (swift) is the near-synonym trap and the one most likely to be chosen by a solver who has got as far as a speed word and stopped there; English does not put swift with trade in this frame. All four options are single adjectives from the speed-and-briskness field, so nothing but the collocation separates them.

Key B. The frame is chairs that had ___ there since breakfast: a past perfect, a plural subject, no object, and a locative adverb, so it requires the past participle of intransitive LIE, which is lain. A (lie) is the bare form and cannot follow had; it catches a solver who has chosen a meaning rather than a form. C (laid) is the participle of transitive LAY and would need something that had been laid; it is the commonest error in this pair and should collect most of the wrong answers. D (lay) is the simple past of LIE, correct in the chairs lay there but not after the auxiliary had. All four options are forms of the LIE/LAY pair, so meaning alone settles nothing: only the morphology of the perfect selects a single answer.

Key C. The preceding sentence gives what the pitch is transactionally, a chair hire and the price of one, and the gapped sentence gives what it actually amounts to on that mile of beach, so the connective has to mark the move from nominal description to observed reality: In practice. A (In principle) is the polarity mirror of that relation, presenting the staffed-presence fact as the theoretical side of the contrast when the passage offers it as the real one. B (In addition) is the additive trap and the choice of a solver who reads the two sentences as a list of facts about the pitch; it would set the staffed presence beside the hire as one more item, when the paragraph, following the earlier statement that what the pitch charges for and what it does are not the same thing, sets the two against each other. D (In short) presents the gapped sentence as a condensation of the one before it, but the sentence condenses nothing; it introduces the mile, the staffing and Gregson, all of them new. All four options are two-word connective adverbials opening with In, each attested sentence-initially before a comma and a full clause, so shape gives nothing away and the gap turns entirely on which discourse relation the two sentences stand in.

Key A. The frame has her pressed on whether she minds, which sets up a question she is being made to answer, and what follows is a two-sided admission that spoils a flattering reading of her job, so the reporting verb must be one of yielding a point: concedes. B (boasts) is the attitude mirror and would turn an unglamorous admission into a claim of pride. C (volunteers) is contradicted by the frame itself, since nothing can be volunteered that has just been pressed for. D (confesses) is the register trap and the hardest of the three: grammatically perfect and roughly the right direction, but confessing requires something owned up to, a fault, a secret or a discreditable feeling, and the sentence itself classifies what she grants as a description rather than a complaint; a description of what the job consists of, an interruption in August and most of the work by late September, is a point conceded to the questioner, not a guilty admission. All four options are third-person singular present-tense reporting verbs agreeing with the subject she, and all four take a that-clause, so grammar decides nothing and the gap is settled by stance and register.

Key D. The clause is built on an explicit contrast, well signed and free, then but, and the sentence closes with the point shutting after one further summer, so the gap takes the negative pole; of the two negative-pole options only barely is a degree adverb English puts before used in this sense. A (widely) is the positive-pole collocation trap: widely used is a fixed phrase, and it is the choice of a solver who reads the counter, the leaflet rack and the paid assistant as evidence of success and skims the but. C (strongly) is the same misreading of polarity with a collocation error on top: English puts strongly with advised, worded and opposed, not with the extent to which a thing is used, and a solver who wants an intensifier for used and does not know the collocation reaches for it. B (scantily) has the right polarity and is the hardest of the three, the form trap for scarcely: scantily describes how thinly something is provided or covered, as in scantily furnished, and does not measure how seldom a counter is resorted to. All four options are single adverbs ending in -ly and each is grammatical before the participle used, so the set splits two and two, two minimisers against two extent adverbs and two live collocations against two dead ones; polarity alone leaves barely and scantily, collocation alone leaves barely and widely, and only a solver who reads the but and knows the collocation reaches the key.
